Keyboard modifier settings on the device vs zh-Hans listing copy — two different jobs

Teams assume keyboard accessibility awareness covers storefront language. iOS, macOS, and App Store Connect actually separate system keyboard modifiers from product-page copy:

  • Sticky Keys on the device — press Shift, Control, Option, and Command one at a time instead of holding modifier chords. Toggle under Settings → Accessibility → Keyboards → Sticky Keys. zh-Hans Settings label: 粘滞键. System Accessibility behavior — outside AppLocale scope.
  • Slow Keys on the device — delay between physical key press and when the key is accepted, reducing accidental keystrokes. Toggle under Settings → Accessibility → Keyboards → Slow Keys. zh-Hans Settings label: 慢速键. Runtime input filtering — not listing rewrite.
  • Mouse Keys on the device — move the pointer using the numeric keypad when a physical mouse or trackpad is difficult to use. Toggle under Settings → Accessibility → Keyboards → Mouse Keys. zh-Hans Settings label: 鼠标键. Pointer movement via keypad — not Pointer Control tracking-speed sliders.
  • Keyboard-modifier marketing on the product page — description paragraphs, subtitle positioning, keywords, promotional text, and screenshot overlays that tell buyers your app works with Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, Mouse Keys, or 辅助功能键盘 workflows. Connect text fields — this page.
  • Pricing and Availability → China — makes the app downloadable on the China storefront. Separate from language rows.
  • App Store tab → Chinese (Simplified) localization — independent row for title, subtitle, keywords, description, promotional text, and screenshot caption lines. Empty or English here means China buyers see English fallback regardless of how strongly your US listing markets Sticky Keys.

A keyboard-modifier-friendly app and a localized China listing are both valuable — neither replaces the other. AppLocale covers how you describe Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, and Mouse Keys benefits on the store page, not whether your code implements keyboard event filtering or numeric keypad pointer handlers at runtime.

What Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, and Mouse Keys actually do — listing honesty

Apple ships keyboard modifier accessibility on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. AppLocale rewrites listing copy from what your US page already claims:

  • Sticky Keys — users press Shift, Control, Option, and Command individually; the system holds each modifier until the next non-modifier key or click. zh-Hans copy can describe 粘滞键 when your English gallery shows Sticky Keys toggles — not generic "keyboard accessibility does everything" superlatives.
  • Slow Keys — users must hold a key for a set duration before it registers, filtering accidental taps. Mention 慢速键 and delay sliders only when your English listing or screenshots already frame those steps.
  • Mouse Keys — users move and click the pointer with numeric keypad keys when a mouse or trackpad is impractical. Mention 鼠标键 and keypad demos only when your English source claims Mouse Keys — not Pointer Control mouse tuning vocabulary.
  • Honest separation from engineering — do not claim your app is Sticky Keys or ships system-wide keyboard modifier infrastructure unless your English source already makes that precise claim; AppLocale aligns zh-Hans strings to your English scope.

Clear zh-Hans keyboard-modifier marketing helps motor-accessibility buyers understand your story before install. It does not replace keyboard event handling code in the binary, modifier-flag detection, or Apple's review decisions.

Sticky Keys–specific listing vocabulary — what translates differently

Keyboard-modifier marketing on App Store pages uses vocabulary general utility guides rarely cover. zh-Hans copy should reflect how Chinese buyers describe Sticky Keys in iOS and macOS Settings — not a literal paste of US keyboard marketing:

Official Settings vocabulary

Apple's zh-Hans Settings UI uses 粘滞键 for Sticky Keys, 慢速键 for Slow Keys, and 鼠标键 for Mouse Keys under Settings → Accessibility → Keyboards (辅助功能 → 键盘). Broader commerce phrasing may use 辅助功能键盘 when marketing the keyboard accessibility family together. Listing copy should mirror that vocabulary — not Full Keyboard Access 完整键盘访问 superlatives or Pointer Control 指针控制 claims when your app only references modifier-key toggles.

Sticky Keys vs Full Keyboard Access

Full Keyboard Access navigates the entire device UI with an external keyboard — Tab, arrow keys, shortcuts, focus ring — 完整键盘访问. Sticky Keys changes how modifier keys register when typing — 粘滞键. Do not keyword-stuff 完整键盘访问 when English only showed Sticky Keys under Accessibility → Keyboards. See our Full Keyboard Access listing guide when external keyboard navigation is your marketing scope.

Mouse Keys vs Pointer Control

Mouse Keys moves the pointer with the numeric keypad — 鼠标键 under Accessibility → Keyboards. Pointer Control tunes external mouse and trackpad tracking speed, scrolling speed, and pointer size — 指针控制. Match the input method your English listing and screenshots actually show.

Slow Keys vs Typing Feedback

Slow Keys filters accidental keystrokes with a press-and-hold delay — 慢速键. Typing Feedback speaks characters and words aloud while typing — 键入反馈 under Spoken Content. Different Settings branches and different screenshot vocabulary.

Subtitle and keyword packing

The 30-character subtitle and 100-character keyword field need keyboard-modifier search terms Chinese buyers type — see Simplified Chinese keywords & subtitle for field mechanics. Terms like 粘滞键, 慢速键, and 鼠标键 each signal different intent from Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, or custom keyboard keywords.

Caption lines vs burned-in badges

Marketing screenshot overlays you control — "Sticky Keys" headlines on gallery frames showing Settings → Accessibility → Keyboards — are separate caption fields or burned-in PNG text. See Screenshot captions in Simplified Chinese for caption-field mechanics when overlays are editable in Connect.

AppLocale FAQ

What are Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, and Mouse Keys — and why does listing copy matter?

Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, and Mouse Keys are under Settings → Accessibility → Keyboards. Sticky Keys lets users press modifier keys one at a time. Slow Keys adds delay before key acceptance. Mouse Keys moves the pointer with the numeric keypad. Marketing those features on your en-US page does not auto-fill zh-Hans Connect fields.

Is Sticky Keys the same as Full Keyboard Access?

No. Full Keyboard Access covers external keyboard Tab-and-arrow navigation, keyboard shortcuts, and focus ring — 完整键盘访问. Sticky Keys covers modifier-key chords pressed one at a time — 粘滞键. See our Full Keyboard Access listing guide for external keyboard navigation claims.

Is Mouse Keys the same as Pointer Control?

No. Mouse Keys uses the numeric keypad to move the pointer — 鼠标键 under Accessibility → Keyboards. Pointer Control tunes external mouse and trackpad tracking speed and pointer size — 指针控制. See our Pointer Control listing guide for pointer-device tuning claims.

No. Slow Keys and Mouse Keys are folded onto this Sticky Keys-as-lead page. One AppLocale SKU delivers paste-ready zh-Hans copy for whichever keyboard-modifier workflows your English listing already claims.
